On the annotation quality side, \citet{baumann2025} demonstrated that 31\% of hypotheses yield incorrect conclusions with LLM annotations, \citet{kim_garg2025} showed 60\% error correlation across models, and \citet{messing2026} decomposed LLM pipeline variance but explicitly excluded causal identification. These works either restrict to binary labels, cover a single topology, or diagnose annotation quality without connecting it to causal estimate validity. Our framework bridges this gap: we provide the causal-analytic link from multi-class confusion matrix structure to topology-specific bias, sensitivity, and correction.

-Our ASV framework draws on the tradition of sensitivity analysis for unmeasured confounding~\cite{rosenbaum2002}. \citet{vanderweele_ding2017} introduced E-values as interpretable sensitivity measures: the minimum strength of unmeasured confounding needed to explain away an observed association. \citet{ding_vanderweele2016} developed assumption-free sensitivity bounds, and \citet{smith_vanderweele2021} proposed bounds for multiple bias sources including misclassification. Our ASVs adapt the E-value philosophy to a different bias source: rather than quantifying unmeasured confounding strength, ASVs quantify the annotation error amplification $\delta$ needed to reach a dangerous bias threshold---with three complementary measures tailored to topology-dependent failure modes (magnitude, significance, and sign-flip).

Prediction-powered inference~\cite{angelopoulos2023} and design-based supervised learning~\cite{egami_hinck_stewart_wei2023, gligoric2025} provide general frameworks for valid inference with ML-generated labels, combining predicted labels with small gold-standard samples. \citet{zrnic_candes2024} extended PPI via cross-prediction for improved efficiency. \citet{audinet2025} benchmarked these methods across datasets. These correction methods are designed as general-purpose tools, agnostic to DAG topology. Our contribution reveals that this agnosticism is costly: correction effectiveness is itself topology-dependent, with matrix-based methods provably ineffective for four of seven topologies. Our ASV analysis identifies \emph{when} correction is needed and \emph{which} failure mode to address, while PPI/DSL provide the \emph{how}.

lines: We presented the first systematic characterization of how multi-class annotation errors interact with causal DAG topology. Our bias taxonomy across seven topologies reveals that the classical binary guarantee of bias toward the null breaks for $K \geq 3$: exposure and IV topologies can produce sign reversal (83.4\% and 52.6\% respectively), while five topologies maintain a structural guarantee of no sign flip. The ASV framework provides topology-aware sensitivity diagnostics, revealing a vulnerability spectrum from IV (maximally fragile) to M-bias (immune). Our correction guidance analysis reveals that correction method effectiveness is itself topology-dependent: a Frisch--Waugh--Lovell invariance result proves matrix-based corrections are ineffective for four topologies, while PPI++ achieves 93.8\% bias reduction at the cost of gold-standard labels. Binarization collapse analysis further demonstrates that simplifying multi-class annotations to binary introduces additional bias varying 147$\times$ across topologies.

-Our framework assumes non-differential misclassification: $P(A^*|A, Y, \mathbf{Z}) = P(A^*|A)$. This holds when the LLM annotator has no access to the outcome $Y$, but may be violated when few-shot examples are selected conditional on $Y$ or when annotation difficulty varies with the outcome. 1	\section{Experiments}
2	\label{sec:experiments}
3	
4	We evaluate the multi-class bias taxonomy and ASV framework through analytical derivations validated by Monte Carlo simulation, covering seven canonical DAG topologies under $K{=}3$ non-differential misclassification.
5	
6	\subsection{Setup}
7	\label{sec:setup}
8	
9	We study seven DAG topologies where annotation variable $A$ enters at structurally distinct positions: confounding, exposure, mediation, collider, M-bias, front-door, and instrumental variable (IV). For each topology, we sample $K{\times}K$ confusion matrices from a Dirichlet$(1,1,1)$ prior (each column independently), generating 100{,}000 random matrices per configuration. Each matrix defines a non-differential misclassification mechanism $C_{jk} = P(A^*{=}j \mid A{=}k)$.
10	
11	For every sampled $C$, we compute the analytical probability limit of the causal estimator and validate it against Monte Carlo simulation with $N{=}10{,}000$ samples per replication. ASV experiments use the parameterization $C(\delta) = (1{-}\delta)I + \delta C_0$, where $\delta{=}0$ recovers perfect classification and $\delta{=}1$ yields the reference matrix $C_0$.
12	
13	\subsection{Bias Taxonomy}
14	\label{sec:taxonomy_results}
15	
16	\paragraph{Theory-MC agreement.}
17	Analytical probability limits match Monte Carlo estimates within 95\% confidence intervals across all seven topologies and all sampled confusion matrices, confirming the closed-form bias expressions derived in Section~\ref{sec:method}.
18	
19	\paragraph{Exposure DAG: catastrophic sign reversal.}
20	Under the full Dirichlet$(1,1,1)$ prior, 85\% of $K{=}3$ confusion matrices produce bias that violates the binary ``toward-null'' guarantee. More critically, 83.4\% of matrices cause \emph{sign reversal} of at least one coefficient. The two failure modes are distinct: for a coefficient with true value $\beta_1{=}1.0$, a near-permutation $C$ produces $\hat{\gamma}_1{=}{-}0.84$ (sign reversal, magnitude $0.84{\times}$); for $\beta_2{=}{-}0.5$, the same $C$ yields $\hat{\gamma}_2{=}{-}1.41$ (same-sign amplification, $2.83{\times}$).
21	
22	This finding persists in practically relevant subspaces. When restricting to confusion matrices with diagonal entries $\geq 0.7$ (typical of current LLM classifiers achieving $F_1 > 0.8$), the violation rate remains 13.7\% with 2.1\% sign reversal and 11.7\% amplification. Even at diagonal $\geq 0.9$, violation persists at 11.9\%. In contrast, the $K{=}2$ control confirms that all six tested binary confusion matrices maintain the classical bias-toward-null guarantee~\cite{brenner1993}, establishing that the multi-class failure is structurally distinct from the binary case.
23	
24	\paragraph{Structural guarantee for non-exposure topologies.}
25	Five of seven topologies exhibit a structural guarantee: $\tau$-specific sign flip rate equals exactly zero across all sampled confusion matrices (Table~\ref{tab:taxonomy}). Confounding, mediation, and front-door topologies show 100\% violation and amplification rates but never reverse the sign of the target causal parameter. Collider misclassification attenuates the spurious association induced by conditioning, providing a form of protection. M-bias shows the weakest sensitivity overall (53.2\% violation, 10.4\% amplification) because annotation error on a collider variable reduces, rather than amplifies, the spurious M-bias path.
26	
27	\paragraph{IV: Wald estimator instability.}
28	The instrumental variable topology is the sole exception among non-exposure DAGs. The Wald estimator's first stage involves $C$ directly in the denominator, and 52.6\% of random confusion matrices cause the denominator to change sign, producing $\tau$-specific sign reversal. This rate remains stable across $K{=}3,5,7$, indicating that IV fragility is a structural property of the Wald estimator rather than a finite-$K$ artifact.
29	
30	\paragraph{Cross-$K$ robustness.}
31	Experiments at $K{=}5$ and $K{=}7$ (100{,}000 random matrices per topology) confirm that all structural patterns from $K{=}3$ persist. The sign-flip guarantee holds for the same five topologies, and IV sign-flip rates remain within 51--53\%. lines: -The epidemiology literature has long studied misclassification bias through causal diagrams~\cite{gustafson2004}. \citet{hernan_cole2009} formalized the starred-node DAG framework for reasoning about measurement bias, distinguishing differential from non-differential error. For binary variables, \citet{ogburn_vanderweele2012} proved that non-differential confounder misclassification produces adjusted estimates between the crude and true values, precluding sign reversal. \citet{brenner1993} showed this guarantee breaks for polytomous confounders, and \citet{veirod_laake2001} derived bias expressions for multi-category exposure misclassification in Poisson regression. \citet{edwards_lessler_naimi2021} further demonstrated that dependent misclassification of covariate and exposure can bias in either direction. However, none of these works systematically characterize how bias varies \emph{across} DAG topologies for a given confusion matrix. Our taxonomy fills this gap: given the same $K$-class confusion matrix, we derive how bias direction and magnitude differ across seven canonical topologies.

+The statistical foundations of measurement error are established in \citet{carroll2006} and \citet{gustafson2004}, with the starred-node DAG framework for reasoning about measurement bias formalized by \citet{hernan_cole2009}. For binary variables, non-differential misclassification biases estimates toward the null~\cite{brenner1993, ogburn_vanderweele2012}. \citet{dosemeci1990} first demonstrated that this guarantee fails for polytomous exposures, and \citet{jurek2005} clarified that the toward-null intuition is frequently misapplied when $K \geq 3$. \citet{veirod_laake2001} derived bias expressions for multi-category exposure misclassification in Poisson regression, and \citet{edwards_lessler_naimi2021} showed that dependent misclassification can bias in either direction. However, all of these works analyze bias within a single DAG topology. Our taxonomy is the first to systematically characterize how the \emph{same} $K$-class confusion matrix produces qualitatively different bias across seven canonical topologies.
\paragraph{Text classifiers and LLM annotation in causal studies.}

-\citet{wood_doughty2018} first applied DAG reasoning to text classifier measurement error. \citet{teblunthuis2024} provided the most complete binary treatment: four DAG scenarios with testable conditions and a Maximum Likelihood Adjustment method, but restricted to binary classification. \citet{lee_wood_doughty2024} extended to categorical LLM classifiers but covered only unobserved confounding. On the annotation quality side, \citet{baumann2025} demonstrated that 31\% of hypotheses yield incorrect conclusions with LLM annotations, \citet{kim_garg2025} showed 60\% error correlation across models, and \citet{messing2026} decomposed LLM pipeline variance but explicitly excluded causal identification. These works either restrict to binary labels, cover a single topology, or diagnose annotation quality without connecting it to causal estimate validity. Our framework bridges this gap: we provide the causal-analytic link from multi-class confusion matrix structure to topology-specific bias, sensitivity, and correction.

+\citet{grimmer2022} provide the methodological foundation for using text as data in social science, while \citet{wood_doughty2018} first applied DAG reasoning to text classifier measurement error. \citet{teblunthuis2024} provided the most complete binary treatment: four DAG scenarios with testable conditions and a Maximum Likelihood Adjustment method, but restricted to $K{=}2$. \citet{lee_wood_doughty2024} extended to categorical LLM classifiers but covered only unobserved confounding. On the annotation quality side, \citet{baumann2025} demonstrated that 31\% of hypotheses yield incorrect conclusions with LLM annotations, \citet{kim_garg2025} showed 60\% error correlation across models, and \citet{messing2026} decomposed LLM pipeline variance but excluded causal identification. These works either restrict to binary labels, cover a single topology, or diagnose annotation quality without connecting it to causal estimate validity. Our framework provides the missing causal-analytic link from multi-class confusion matrix structure to topology-specific bias, sensitivity, and correction.

-Our ASV framework draws on the tradition of sensitivity analysis for unmeasured confounding~\cite{rosenbaum2002}. \citet{vanderweele_ding2017} introduced E-values as interpretable sensitivity measures: the minimum strength of unmeasured confounding needed to explain away an observed association. \citet{ding_vanderweele2016} developed assumption-free sensitivity bounds, and \citet{smith_vanderweele2021} proposed bounds for multiple bias sources including misclassification. Our ASVs adapt the E-value philosophy to a different bias source: rather than quantifying unmeasured confounding strength, ASVs quantify the annotation error amplification $\delta$ needed to reach a dangerous bias threshold. Unlike the scalar E-value, ASVs comprise three complementary types (magnitude, significance, and sign-flip), because annotation error failure modes are topology-dependent.

+Our ASV framework draws on two traditions. First, \citet{rosenbaum2002} established sensitivity analysis for unmeasured confounding, and \citet{vanderweele_ding2017} introduced E-values as interpretable scalar measures of the minimum confounding strength needed to explain away an observed association. \citet{ding_vanderweele2016} developed assumption-free sensitivity bounds, and \citet{smith_vanderweele2021} proposed bounds for multiple bias sources. Second, \citet{lash2009} developed probabilistic bias analysis (PBA) using confusion matrices as sensitivity parameters for misclassification. Our ASVs differ from both traditions in several ways: unlike the scalar E-value, ASVs comprise three complementary types (magnitude, significance, and sign-flip), because annotation error failure modes are topology-dependent; unlike PBA's simulation-based approach for binary settings, ASVs provide formal monotonicity and sharpness guarantees over $K{\times}K$ confusion matrices; and ASVs yield a single scalar report ($\delta^*$) per topology, facilitating communication alongside standard causal estimates.

-Prediction-powered inference~\cite{angelopoulos2023} and design-based supervised learning~\cite{egami_hinck_stewart_wei2023, gligoric2025} provide general frameworks for valid inference with ML-generated labels, combining predicted labels with small gold-standard samples. \citet{zrnic_candes2024} extended PPI via cross-prediction for improved efficiency. \citet{audinet2025} benchmarked these methods across datasets. These correction methods are designed as general-purpose tools, agnostic to DAG topology. Our contribution reveals that this agnosticism is costly: correction effectiveness is itself topology-dependent, with matrix-based methods provably ineffective for four of seven topologies. Our ASV analysis identifies \emph{when} correction is needed and \emph{which} failure mode to address, while PPI/DSL provide the \emph{how}.

+Prediction-powered inference (PPI++)~\cite{angelopoulos2023} and design-based supervised learning (DSL)~\cite{egami_hinck_stewart_wei2023, gligoric2025} provide general frameworks for valid inference with ML-generated labels. \citet{zrnic_candes2024} extended PPI via cross-prediction, and \citet{audinet2025} benchmarked these methods across datasets. These tools are designed as topology-agnostic. Our contribution reveals that this agnosticism is costly: correction effectiveness is itself topology-dependent, with matrix-based methods provably ineffective for four of seven topologies. Our ASV analysis identifies \emph{when} correction is needed and \emph{which} failure mode to address, while PPI/DSL provide the \emph{how}.

1	\section{Introduction}
2	\label{sec:introduction}
3	
4	Large language models are rapidly replacing human annotators in computational social science, with researchers using LLM-generated labels for tasks ranging from sentiment classification to political stance detection~\cite{gilardi2023chatgpt, ziems2024can, egami_hinck_stewart_wei2023, baumann2025}. Crucially, most of these tasks are inherently multi-class: stance detection uses 3--4 categories, sentiment analysis 5, and disaster response taxonomies 10 or more. This shift promises dramatic cost reduction, but introduces a critical validity gap: annotation errors from imperfect classifiers propagate into downstream causal estimates in ways that depend on both the error structure and the causal design. \citet{baumann2025} demonstrate that across 37 annotation tasks, 31\% of hypotheses yield incorrect conclusions with state-of-the-art LLMs, rising to 50\% for smaller models; these errors are highly correlated across models (60\% agreement when both err)~\cite{kim_garg2025}, undermining ensemble-based mitigation. Analyzing the \emph{structure} of annotation error, rather than simply reducing its magnitude, is essential for valid downstream inference.
5	
6	Even under realistic classifier accuracy (diagonal $\geq 0.7$), 13.7\% of $K{=}3$ confusion matrices violate the classical binary guarantee, with 2.1\% causing sign reversal of the estimated treatment effect. Across the full Dirichlet$(1,1,1)$ parameter space, sign reversal reaches 83.4\%. This breaks the guarantee that non-differential misclassification biases estimates ``toward the null''~\cite{brenner1993}, a guarantee that many applied researchers implicitly rely upon. Standard classification metrics do not predict this risk: within a narrow $F_1$ range of 0.614--0.690 across three frontier LLMs, relative bias varies by an order of magnitude across topologies (from 4.1\% to 42.1\%), illustrating that \emph{topology}, not annotator quality, determines downstream risk.
7	
8	The mechanism is algebraic, and the transition at $K {\geq} 3$ is a qualitative break, not a gradual degradation. For $K{=}2$, the stochastic constraint forces any confusion matrix with $C_{kk} {>} 0.5$ to preserve coefficient signs---an algebraic property of the $2{\times}2$ matrix dimension, not of a specific error rate. This guarantee \emph{vanishes} at $K {\geq} 3$: the higher-dimensional confusion matrix admits negative effective weights on categories with opposite-sign coefficients, enabling sign reversal even when every diagonal entry exceeds $0.5$~\cite{veirod_laake2001}. This fundamental asymmetry has received limited systematic treatment. \citet{brenner1993} identified the possibility of polytomous reversal but did not characterize it across causal designs. \citet{lee_wood_doughty2024} extended classifier error analysis to categorical variables and LLM classifiers, but covered only one DAG topology (unobserved confounding). The possibility of polytomous sign reversal was noted by \citet{dosemeci1990} and \citet{veirod_laake2001}; our contribution extends this to a systematic characterization across seven DAG topologies and provides the ASV framework for quantifying vulnerability.
9	
10	We address these gaps with three contributions:
11	
12	\begin{enumerate}
13	\item \textbf{Multi-class bias taxonomy.} We derive bias expressions for seven canonical DAG topologies (Figure~\ref{fig:dag_taxonomy}) under $K$-class non-differential misclassification, prove sign preservation for confounding and collider, verify it numerically for mediation, M-bias, and front-door, and show that exposure and IV can produce sign reversal. Binarization amplifies the gap: collapsing $K{=}3$ to binary introduces additional bias varying 154$\times$ across topologies.
14	
15	\item \textbf{Annotation Sensitivity Values (ASVs).} We propose three complementary sensitivity measures---magnitude, significance, and sign-flip ASV---revealing a vulnerability spectrum from IV (maximally fragile, 52.6\% sign reversal) to M-bias (immune, ASV $= \infty$).

17	\item \textbf{Topology-aware correction guidance.} We evaluate five correction methods and show that matrix-based corrections achieve exactly 0\% bias reduction for four topologies due to Frisch--Waugh--Lovell invariance.
